topics.name: Algebra
topics.description: Algebra is the language the rest of math is written in. Learn to isolate variables, read the slope of a line, factor expressions, and use the quadratic formula without second-guessing every sign.
topics.imageAlt: Handwritten algebra equations on grid paper

formulas.name: Solving Linear Equations
formulas.formula: ax + b = c  →  x = (c − b) ÷ a
formulas.summary: Undo the operations around x in reverse order until x is alone on one side of the equals sign.
formulas.whenToUse: Any equation where x appears only to the first power, such as 3x + 5 = 20 or 7 − 2x = 1.
formulas.watchOut: Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other. Undo addition and subtraction before multiplication and division.

steps.title: Identify the parts
steps.text: Write the equation and spot what is happening to x: it is multiplied by 3, then 5 is added. We will undo those in reverse order.

steps.title: Subtract 5 from both sides
steps.text: The last thing done to x was "+ 5", so undo it first. Subtracting 5 from both sides keeps the equation balanced.

steps.title: Divide both sides by 3
steps.text: Now x is multiplied by 3. Divide both sides by 3 to get x by itself.

steps.title: Check your answer
steps.text: Plug x = 5 back into the original equation. If both sides match, the answer is correct.

formulas.name: Slope and Slope-Intercept Form
formulas.formula: m = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁),   y = mx + b
formulas.summary: Slope (m) measures how steep a line is: rise over run. Once you know m and one point, you can find the y-intercept (b) and write the line's equation.
formulas.whenToUse: You are given two points and need the equation of the line through them, or need to describe a constant rate of change.
formulas.watchOut: Subtract in the same order on top and bottom. If you start with y₂ on top, you must start with x₂ on the bottom.

steps.title: Label your points
steps.text: Call one point (x₁, y₁) and the other (x₂, y₂). It does not matter which is which, as long as you stay consistent.

steps.title: Plug into the slope formula
steps.text: Rise over run: the change in y divided by the change in x, subtracting in the same order on top and bottom.

steps.title: Simplify the slope
steps.text: The line rises 4 units for every 2 units it runs to the right, so the slope is 2.

steps.title: Solve for b
steps.text: Substitute m = 2 and either point into y = mx + b, then solve for b. Here we use (1, 3).

steps.title: Write the equation
steps.text: Put m and b back into slope-intercept form. You can check it with the other point: 2(3) + 1 = 7 ✓.

formulas.name: Factoring Trinomials
formulas.formula: x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q),  where p · q = c and p + q = b
formulas.summary: Factoring rewrites a trinomial as a product of two binomials. You are looking for two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.
formulas.whenToUse: Simplifying expressions, solving quadratics that factor nicely, and canceling terms in fractions (you'll need it in calculus limits too).
formulas.watchOut: The pair has to satisfy both conditions. Many pairs multiply to c, but only one also adds to b. Watch the signs when c is negative.

steps.title: Identify b and c
steps.text: Compare the trinomial to x² + bx + c. The middle coefficient is b and the constant is c.

steps.title: List factor pairs of c
steps.text: Write every pair of whole numbers that multiplies to 6, then check which pair adds to 5.

steps.title: Write the factors
steps.text: The winning pair is 2 and 3, so each goes into its own binomial with x.

steps.title: Check by multiplying (FOIL)
steps.text: Multiply the binomials back out. If you get the original trinomial, the factoring is correct.

formulas.name: The Quadratic Formula
formulas.summary: The quadratic formula solves any equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, even when it will not factor.
formulas.whenToUse: Whenever you have a quadratic set equal to zero and factoring is hard or impossible.
formulas.watchOut: Keep the sign of every coefficient (c = −2, not 2). The whole numerator is divided by 2a, not just the square root. The ± means there are usually two answers.

steps.title: Identify a, b, and c
steps.text: Make sure the equation equals zero, then read off the coefficients, signs included.

steps.title: Compute the discriminant
steps.text: The part under the square root, b² − 4ac, is called the discriminant. Work it out first so the rest stays tidy. Two negatives multiply to a positive.

steps.title: Plug into the formula
steps.text: Substitute b, the discriminant, and a. The square root of 25 is 5.

steps.title: Split the ±
steps.text: Do the problem once with + and once with −. Each gives one solution.

steps.title: Check a solution
steps.text: Plug a solution back in to confirm it gives zero. On the graph, both solutions are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.

topics.name: Geometry
topics.description: Geometry is about the size and shape of things. Learn the formulas for right triangles, areas, circles, and volume, and how to tell which measurement goes where.
topics.imageAlt: A drafting compass drawing a circle on paper

formulas.name: The Pythagorean Theorem
formulas.summary: In a right triangle, the squares of the two legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse (the longest side).
formulas.whenToUse: Finding a missing side of a right triangle, or the straight-line distance between two points.
formulas.watchOut: c is always the hypotenuse, the side across from the right angle. Square each side before adding; (3 + 4)² is not the same as 3² + 4².
formulas.example: Legs of 3 and 4. Find the hypotenuse.

steps.title: Label the sides
steps.text: The two sides that form the right angle are the legs, a and b. The side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse, c.

steps.title: Substitute into the formula
steps.text: Replace a and b with the leg lengths.

steps.title: Square and add
steps.text: Square each leg first, then add the results.

steps.title: Take the square root
steps.text: c² is 25, so c is the positive square root of 25. Side lengths are never negative.

formulas.name: Area of a Triangle
formulas.summary: A triangle is exactly half of a rectangle with the same base and height, so its area is half of base times height.
formulas.whenToUse: Finding the area of any triangle when you know a base and the height to that base.
formulas.watchOut: The height must be perpendicular (at 90°) to the base. It is usually not one of the slanted sides. Area units are squared (cm²).
formulas.example: Base of 8 cm and height of 5 cm

steps.title: Find the base and height
steps.text: Pick a side as the base. The height is the perpendicular distance from that base to the opposite corner (the dashed line).

steps.title: Substitute into the formula
steps.text: Replace b and h with their values.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.text: Multiply base times height, then take half. Because we multiplied cm by cm, the answer is in square centimeters.

formulas.name: Circle Area and Circumference
formulas.summary: Area is the space inside a circle; circumference is the distance around it. Both depend only on the radius, r.
formulas.whenToUse: Any problem with circles: pizza sizes, wheels, round tables, or the curved part of cylinders and cones.
formulas.watchOut: Use the radius, not the diameter. If you are given the diameter, divide it by 2 first. Only r is squared, not π.
formulas.example: A circle with a diameter of 10

steps.title: Find the radius
steps.text: The radius is half the diameter. This is the step people most often skip.

steps.title: Find the area
steps.text: Square the radius, then multiply by π. Leaving the answer as 25π is exact; 78.54 is a rounded decimal.

steps.title: Find the circumference
steps.text: Multiply 2 by π by the radius. (This is the same as π times the diameter.)

steps.title: Label your units
steps.text: Area is measured in square units; circumference is a length, so it uses plain units.

formulas.name: Volume of a Cylinder
formulas.summary: Volume is the area of the circular base stacked up through the height of the cylinder.
formulas.whenToUse: Finding how much a can, pipe, tank, or glass holds.
formulas.watchOut: Find the base area (πr²) before multiplying by the height. Volume units are cubed (cm³).
formulas.example: Radius of 3 cm and height of 10 cm

steps.title: Identify the radius and height
steps.text: The radius goes from the center of the circular base to its edge. The height runs between the two bases.

steps.title: Find the area of the base
steps.text: The base is a circle, so its area is πr².

steps.title: Multiply by the height
steps.text: Stack that base area up 10 cm high.

steps.title: Approximate and label
steps.text: Multiply by π ≈ 3.14159 for a decimal answer. Three lengths multiplied together give cubic units.

topics.name: Calculus
topics.description: Calculus describes how things change. Learn to evaluate limits, take derivatives with the power and chain rules, and find the area under a curve with a definite integral.
topics.imageAlt: A printed graph of a function with labeled axes

formulas.name: Evaluating Limits
formulas.summary: A limit asks what value f(x) approaches as x gets closer and closer to a, even if f(a) itself is undefined.
formulas.whenToUse: When direct substitution gives 0/0, and as the foundation for derivatives.
formulas.watchOut: 0/0 is not an answer. It means "simplify and try again". Factor, cancel, then substitute.

steps.title: Try direct substitution
steps.text: Always try plugging in first. Here we get 0/0, which is called indeterminate. It tells us to simplify.

steps.title: Factor the numerator
steps.text: x² − 4 is a difference of squares, which factors into (x − 2)(x + 2).

steps.title: Cancel the common factor
steps.text: The (x − 2) on top and bottom cancel. This is allowed because a limit never actually uses x = 2.

steps.title: Substitute again
steps.text: Now direct substitution works. The graph is the line y = x + 2 with a hole at x = 2, and the limit is the height of that hole.

formulas.name: The Power Rule
formulas.summary: To differentiate x to a power, bring the exponent down in front and subtract one from the exponent.
formulas.whenToUse: Taking the derivative of any polynomial, and most terms with x raised to a number.
formulas.watchOut: The derivative of a constant is 0, not the constant. Multiply the coefficient by the old exponent before lowering the exponent.

steps.title: Split into terms
steps.text: Derivatives can be taken one term at a time, keeping the plus and minus signs between them.

steps.title: Differentiate 3x⁴
steps.text: Bring the 4 down and multiply it by 3, then subtract 1 from the exponent.

steps.title: Differentiate −5x²
steps.text: Bring the 2 down and multiply it by −5. The exponent drops to 1, so we just write x.

steps.title: Differentiate the constant
steps.text: A constant never changes, so its rate of change (its derivative) is zero.

steps.title: Combine the results
steps.text: Put the term derivatives back together to get the derivative f′(x).

formulas.name: The Chain Rule
formulas.summary: For a function inside another function, take the derivative of the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
formulas.whenToUse: Whenever something more complicated than plain x is raised to a power or placed inside sin, eˣ, ln, √, and so on.
formulas.watchOut: The most common mistake is forgetting to multiply by the inside's derivative, g′(x).

steps.title: Identify outer and inner functions
steps.text: Something is raised to the 5th power: that's the outer function. The something, 3x² + 1, is the inner function. Call it u.

steps.title: Differentiate the outer function
steps.text: Use the power rule on u⁵, treating u as a single block.

steps.title: Differentiate the inner function
steps.text: Use the power rule on 3x² + 1.

steps.title: Multiply and substitute back
steps.text: Multiply the two derivatives, and put 3x² + 1 back in place of u.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.text: Multiply the numbers in front: 5 · 6x = 30x.

formulas.name: Definite Integrals
formulas.summary: A definite integral gives the area under a curve between x = a and x = b. Find an antiderivative F, then subtract F(a) from F(b).
formulas.whenToUse: Finding area under a curve, total distance from a velocity, or any total accumulated over an interval.
formulas.watchOut: Subtract in the right order: upper limit minus lower limit. To check an antiderivative, take its derivative and see if you get f(x) back.

steps.title: Find the antiderivative
steps.text: Reverse the power rule: add 1 to each exponent and divide by the new exponent. 3x² becomes x³ and 2x becomes x².

steps.title: Evaluate at the upper limit
steps.text: Plug the top number, b = 2, into F(x).

steps.title: Evaluate at the lower limit
steps.text: Plug the bottom number, a = 0, into F(x).

steps.title: Subtract
steps.text: Upper minus lower. The shaded area under the curve from 0 to 2 is 12 square units.
